analogy.p: Think of the coast as a factory: weathering is a team that loosens bricks in a wall, erosion is a sandblaster that wears the wall down, transportation is a conveyor belt (longshore drift) carrying the debris along the shore, and deposition is the loading bay where the belt stops and the goods are stacked up as a beach. This maps the idea of energy and material moving through a system. It breaks down because in the real coast the 'factory' has no owner or plan: the sandblaster, belt and loading bay change with every storm, tide and wind direction.
analogy.t: A beach as a conveyor belt and a sandpaper factory

bullets: **Weathering** = the breakdown of rock **in situ** (in place), with no movement of the material.
**Mass movement** = the downhill movement of material under gravity (sliding, slumping, rockfall).
**Erosion** = the wearing away of the land by a moving agent (waves) carrying rock particles.
**Transportation** = the movement of eroded material by the sea.
**Deposition** = the dropping of material when the sea loses energy.
Keep the key distinction: **weathering does not involve a moving agent**, erosion does.
Rates vary with **wave energy, rock type, geological structure, fetch and human activity**.
core.h: The coast as a system of processes
core.p: A coast is the zone where land meets sea. Its shape at any moment is the result of a balance between **destructive** processes that remove material (weathering, mass movement, erosion) and **constructive** processes that add material (transportation and deposition). The spec asks you to know the work of each of these physical processes, the two main wave types, and how they combine. Understanding them is essential because every coastal landform you study later (cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches, stacks, beaches, spits, bars) is produced by these processes acting on different rock types.

bullets: **Fetch**: the longer the fetch, the larger and more powerful the waves. The UK's south and west coasts face the Atlantic, so they have long fetch and powerful waves.
**Wind strength and duration**: stronger, longer storms create bigger waves.
**Swash**: the forward movement of water up the beach after a wave breaks.
**Backwash**: the return of water down the beach under gravity.
**Wave height** and **wavelength** vary; the **frequency** is the number of waves per minute.
As waves enter shallow water they are slowed down at the base; the wave steepens and then collapses (**breaks**).
**Storm waves** release huge energy and can cause rapid erosion and flooding, especially if combined with high tides or surges.
core.h: Waves: how they form and what controls their energy
core.p: Waves are caused by **wind blowing over the surface of the sea**. Friction between the wind and the water makes the surface move in a circular motion. As a wave approaches the shore, the bottom of the wave is slowed by friction with the sea bed, so the top spills forwards and the wave **breaks**. After breaking, water rushes up the beach as the **swash** and drains back down under gravity as the **backwash**. The size and power of a wave depend on how strong the wind is, how long it blows for, and the **fetch**, the distance of open water the wind has blown over.

bullets: **Constructive**: low height, long wavelength, **low frequency (about 6 to 8 per minute)**; swash is **stronger** than backwash; deposit material and build up the beach; gently sloping beach.
**Destructive**: high, short wavelength, **high frequency (about 10 to 14 per minute)**; backwash is **stronger** than swash; erode material and remove it from the beach; steep beach profile.
Constructive waves **spill** gently onto the beach; destructive waves **plunge** and crash.
Destructive waves have a short swash and powerful backwash that drags material back out to sea.
Beaches are built by constructive waves in summer (calm) and cut back by destructive waves in winter (stormy), so beach profiles change with the seasons.
Comparing: constructive = deposition, low energy; destructive = erosion, high energy.
The nature of the wave depends on the **fetch, wind and shape of the sea bed**.
core.p: The spec requires you to know two main wave types. **Constructive waves** are low, long and gentle and tend to build beaches by depositing material. **Destructive waves** are high, steep and crash down, which tends to erode beaches and cliffs. The main difference is the balance between swash and backwash, and this is a frequent exam question.

bullets: **Freeze-thaw (frost shattering)**: water enters cracks in the rock; when it freezes at night it **expands by about 9 percent**, putting pressure on the crack; when it thaws the ice melts and the crack gets wider; repeated cycles cause pieces to break off.
Freeze-thaw needs **cracks (joints) in the rock** and **temperatures fluctuating around freezing point**, so it is common on cliffs in winter.
Broken pieces fall to the foot of the cliff as **scree** (talus).
**Salt crystallisation** (**salt weathering**): sea spray evaporates and leaves salt crystals in cracks, which grow and exert pressure.
**Wetting and drying** can cause some rocks like clay and shale to expand and contract.
Mechanical weathering is more effective in **jointed** rocks and in **exposed** cliffs.
Link: freeze-thaw also shapes glaciated uplands, linking to the glacial landscapes topic.
core.p: Weathering is the breakdown of rock where it is, without it being moved. At the coast, weathering weakens cliffs so they are easier to erode. **Mechanical weathering** breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its chemical composition. The main type in the UK is **freeze-thaw weathering**, which operates where temperatures fluctuate around 0 degrees C.

bullets: **Carbonation**: rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and becomes a weak **carbonic acid**; this reacts with calcium carbonate in limestone and chalk to form **calcium hydrogencarbonate**, which is soluble and is washed away.
Equation (Higher/extension): CaCO3 + H2O + CO2 -> Ca(HCO3)2 (calcium hydrogencarbonate, dissolved).
Carbonation only affects **carbonate rocks** (limestone, chalk) and is faster in **cool, wet** conditions because cold water holds more dissolved CO2.
**Oxidation** and **solution** can also weaken rocks, e.g. iron minerals rusting in sandstone.
**Biological weathering**: roots grow into cracks and force them apart; burrowing animals and seabirds create holes; seaweed and algae can secrete chemicals.
Weathering weakens the rock, so waves find it easier to **erode** it; this is why weathering and erosion work together.
core.h: Weathering at the coast: chemical and biological
core.p: **Chemical weathering** changes the chemical composition of the rock, so it breaks down or dissolves. At the coast, the most important is **carbonation weathering** of limestone and chalk, which are made of **calcium carbonate**. **Biological weathering** is caused by living things such as plant roots or burrowing animals.

bullets: **Rockfall**: pieces of rock **break off** a steep cliff face (often following freeze-thaw weathering) and fall to the base to form **scree**; typical of **hard, jointed, steep** cliffs.

**Sliding (landslide)**: a block of material **slides in a straight line** along a flat surface (a bedding plane or joint) that dips towards the sea; happens on cliffs where layers of rock slope seaward.
**Slumping (rotational slip)**: saturated **soft rock** such as clay moves along a **curved** slip plane in a rotational movement, leaving a **terraced, hummocky cliff** profile.
Slumping happens where **permeable rock lies on top of impermeable rock** (e.g. sand or chalk on clay): water cannot drain through, builds up and lubricates the slip plane.
**Causes**: heavy rain, saturated ground, waves undercutting the base, weak rocks, steep slopes, vegetation removal.
**Result**: cliff retreat and a supply of material for the sea to erode and transport.
Example: **Holderness coast** (boulder clay slumping) and **Barton on Sea**, Hampshire (clay slips).
core.h: Mass movement: sliding, slumping and rockfall
core.p: **Mass movement** is the downhill movement of material under the force of gravity. It is often triggered when weathering has weakened a cliff, when the rock becomes saturated with water, or when waves undercut the cliff base. The spec names three types: **rockfall**, **sliding** and **slumping**, and you should be able to describe each and explain where it happens.

bullets: **Hydraulic power (hydraulic action)**: the force of the water crashing against the cliff **forces air into cracks**; the air is compressed, and when the wave retreats the air **expands explosively**, widening the crack and weakening the rock.
**Abrasion (corrasion)**: waves **pick up pebbles and boulders and hurl them** at the cliff, **sandpapering** and chipping away rock; works at the base to form a **wave-cut notch**.
**Attrition**: rocks and pebbles carried by waves **collide and rub against each other**, becoming **smaller, smoother and rounder**; it reduces the size of the load and produces sand.
**Solution (corrosion)**: **dissolving** of soluble minerals (e.g. carbonates in limestone and chalk) in sea water; chemical not physical.

**Factors affecting erosion**: wave energy and fetch, rock type, geological structure (joints, bedding planes, faults), amount and size of load, presence of beaches that absorb wave energy, human protection structures.
Abrasion is the main erosion process on beaches with plenty of shingle; hydraulic power dominates on cliffs with many cracks.
**Cause and effect**: erosion at the cliff base forms a **wave-cut notch**, undercutting leaves the cliff overhanging, and it collapses (mass movement).
core.h: Erosion: hydraulic power, abrasion, attrition and solution
core.p: Erosion is the wearing away of rock by the sea and the load it carries. It is most effective during storms with powerful destructive waves. The spec names three main processes, **hydraulic power**, **abrasion** and **attrition**, and the extra process **solution** (corrosion), and you must be able to explain each in detail.

bullets: **Resistant** rocks (granite, basalt, hard limestone): erode at less than 1 cm per year; form steep cliffs and headlands.

**Less resistant** rocks (clay, shale, sand, boulder clay): erode at metres per year; form low, gently sloping cliffs and bays. **Holderness**, East Yorkshire, loses an average of about **1.8 to 2 m a year**.
**Joints, bedding planes and faults** are lines of weakness that waves exploit by hydraulic power and abrasion.
**Dip** of the rock: rocks dipping towards the sea can slide; rocks dipping inland give steep cliffs.

**Concordant coast**: bands of different rock run **parallel** to the coastline; the hard outer layer protects the soft layer behind it (e.g. Lulworth Cove: after the outer Portland limestone is breached, the soft clay behind erodes into a cove).
**Discordant coast**: bands of different rock run **at right angles** to the coast, giving alternating **headlands (hard)** and **bays (soft)** (e.g. Swanage Bay, Dorset).
Result: **differential erosion** shapes the coastline.
core.h: Rock type and structure: why some coasts erode faster
core.p: Not all coasts erode at the same speed. **Rock type** (lithology) and **geological structure** control how fast erosion happens and what landforms develop. Hard resistant rocks like granite give slow erosion and high, steep cliffs. Soft rocks like clay give rapid erosion and low, crumbling cliffs. **Discordant** and **concordant** coasts are special cases where bands of different rock lie at right angles to or parallel to the coast.

bullets: **Solution**: dissolved minerals (e.g. calcium carbonate) are carried in the water; invisible.
**Suspension**: small particles such as silt and clay are **carried within the water** (makes the sea look muddy).
**Saltation**: larger particles (sand, small pebbles) **bounce** along the sea bed in a series of hops.
**Traction**: the heaviest particles (large pebbles and boulders) are **rolled along** the sea bed.
**Longshore drift**: the movement of material **along the coast** in a zigzag pattern (see next section).
**Wave energy** controls the size of the load that can be transported; storms move large boulders.
Transportation causes attrition, so material gets smaller further along the coast.
core.h: Transportation: how the sea moves material
core.p: Transportation is the movement of eroded material (the **load**) by the sea. The sea can carry material in four main ways, depending on the size and weight of the particles and the energy of the waves. Material is also moved along the coast by **longshore drift**, which is the key process for building beaches, spits and bars.

bullets: **Step 1**: waves approach the coast at an angle because of the prevailing wind direction.
**Step 2**: the **swash** carries pebbles and sand **up the beach at the same angle as the wave**.
**Step 3**: the **backwash** carries the material **straight back down the beach** at right angles to the coast, due to gravity (the steepest slope).
**Step 4**: the repeated swash and backwash move material in a **zigzag** along the beach.
**Step 5**: overall, material moves in **one direction** along the coast (e.g. west to east on the south coast of England).
Where the coast changes direction or enters a river mouth, longshore drift **deposits** material to form a **spit** (e.g. Spurn Head, Dorset's Hurst Castle spit).
**Groynes** are built to trap this material and stop it moving away (coastal management link).
Helps explain why one place has too much sand while another loses its beach.
core.p: Longshore drift moves sand and shingle along the coastline in a zigzag. It happens where waves hit the coast at an **angle**, driven by the **prevailing wind** (in the UK, mainly south-westerly). Waves approach the beach at an angle, push material up the beach in the direction of the wave (swash), but the backwash flows straight back down the steepest slope at right angles to the shore under gravity. Repeating this moves the material along.

bullets: **Conditions for deposition**: low-energy environment, **shallow water**, sheltered bays, **estuaries**, wind or wave direction change, a **lot of material** supplied, constructive waves.
**Heaviest particles** (boulders, large pebbles) are dropped first, and the finest (silt, clay) last; so shingle is found at the top of the beach and sand at the bottom (sorting).
**Beaches** are accumulations of sand or shingle between the high tide and low tide marks; **sandy beaches** are gentle and low, **shingle beaches** are steeper.
**Berms** and **ridges** show high tide marks.
**Spits, bars, tombolos** and **salt marshes** are depositional landforms studied in the later spec point.
Deposition protects the coast because beaches absorb wave energy.
Sources of beach material: erosion of cliffs, material brought by rivers, and material swept onshore from the sea bed.
core.h: Deposition: when and why the sea drops its load
core.p: **Deposition** occurs when the sea **loses energy** and can no longer carry its load. This happens where waves slow down (in sheltered bays, estuaries, behind spits or headlands), when the waves are constructive with a strong swash and weak backwash, or when there is a large amount of material to move. Deposition builds beaches, spits, bars and tombolos.

bullets: **Sediment cell**: a length of coastline and its nearshore area where sediment movement is largely self-contained.
**Inputs**: cliff erosion, river sediment, offshore sources; **transfers**: longshore drift, onshore and offshore movement; **outputs**: loss offshore, to deep water or into estuaries.
**Positive sediment budget** = more input than output = beaches grow; **negative** = more output than input = beaches shrink; **balanced** = equilibrium.
**Dynamic equilibrium**: the coast adjusts to changes in inputs and outputs.
Human actions (hard engineering, dredging, dams) can cut sediment supply and increase erosion downdrift.
Link: **coastal management** decisions should consider the whole cell (Shoreline Management Plans).
Exam tip: use the idea of inputs, transfers and outputs when explaining why one coast is eroding while another builds up.
core.h: Sediment cells and the sediment budget
core.p: The coastline of England and Wales is divided into **11 major sediment cells** (and a number of sub-cells). A sediment cell is a stretch of coast within which the movement of sand and shingle is largely **self-contained**, so what is removed from one place usually ends up somewhere else within the same cell. This idea helps managers plan, because building a sea wall in one area can affect erosion elsewhere in the cell.

bullets: **Cliff retreat sequence**: weathering weakens rock -> waves erode the base (notch) -> the cliff is undercut -> collapse (rockfall or slump) -> material removed and transported -> platform widens.
**Wave-cut platform**: the flat rock area left as the cliff retreats; formed by abrasion and then exposed at low tide.
**Wave type matters**: destructive waves erode, constructive waves deposit.
**Rock type and structure** determine which process dominates.
Climate change: rising sea levels and stormier conditions may speed up erosion in the future.
**Human impact**: buildings, sea walls and groynes interfere with processes.
Examiners reward answers that **name the process and explain how it works** rather than just labelling.
core.h: Putting it together: linking processes and landforms
core.p: This spec point is the foundation for all coastal landforms. Weathering and mass movement weaken and cause cliffs to retreat; waves attack the base by hydraulic power and abrasion, forming a wave-cut notch; the material is transported by the sea and longshore drift; and deposition builds beaches and spits elsewhere. The processes interact in a cycle, with feedback: more erosion gives more load, more load gives more abrasion.

exam: **Define/State** questions (1 mark): learn the exact definitions, e.g. 'weathering is the breakdown of rock in situ'.
**Describe** a process (2 to 3 marks): give a clear sequence of steps, e.g. for freeze-thaw: water enters cracks -> freezes and expands -> widens crack -> repeated.
**Explain** (4 marks): use the structure point-because-so: 'Destructive waves have a strong backwash, so material is dragged out to sea, which leads to a steep beach.'
**Compare constructive and destructive waves**: give at least three differences (height, swash/backwash, effect) and use comparative words such as 'whereas' or 'in contrast'.
**Longshore drift** (up to 4 marks): mention prevailing wind, waves at an angle, swash up at an angle, backwash straight down, zigzag, net movement along the coast; a labelled diagram can gain marks.
**6-mark questions** may combine processes with a landform: link process -> effect -> landform, with named examples (e.g. Holderness, Lulworth Cove).
Add **examples with figures** (Holderness 2 m per year) for the top level.
For **data and graph questions** (e.g. erosion rates), quote values with units and describe trends and anomalies.
Watch the **command word**: 'Describe' = what happens; 'Explain' = why; 'Suggest' = apply knowledge to an unfamiliar scenario.

mistakes.r: Weathering breaks down rock in place with no moving agent; erosion involves a moving agent (waves) carrying material away.
mistakes.w: Weathering and erosion are the same thing.

mistakes.r: Specify that water forces air into cracks, the air is compressed then expands as the wave retreats, which widens the crack.
mistakes.w: Hydraulic power is when waves hit the cliff.

mistakes.r: Abrasion wears away the cliff by hurled rock fragments; attrition wears down the load itself so it becomes smaller and rounder.
mistakes.w: Abrasion and attrition are the same.

mistakes.r: It is a zigzag: swash at an angle up the beach, backwash straight down at right angles.
mistakes.w: Longshore drift moves material straight along the beach.

mistakes.r: Destructive waves are higher and steeper; constructive waves are low with a long wavelength.
Destructive waves have a weak swash and strong backwash; constructive waves have a strong swash and weak backwash.
mistakes.w: Destructive waves have a strong swash.

mistakes.r: Water in cracks freezes and expands (about 9 percent), widening the crack; repeated freezing and thawing breaks the rock.
mistakes.w: Freeze-thaw happens because water freezes and the rock freezes.

mistakes.r: Sliding is along a straight (planar) surface; slumping is a rotational movement along a curved slip plane in soft, saturated rock.
mistakes.w: Slumping and sliding are the same.

summary: This spec point asks you to explain the physical processes that shape the UK coast: weathering (mechanical, chemical, biological), mass movement (rockfall, sliding, slumping), erosion (hydraulic power, abrasion, attrition, solution), transportation (traction, saltation, suspension, solution and longshore drift) and deposition, plus the two types of wave. It matters because these processes explain every coastal landform and the case for coastal management.

terms.d: The breakdown of rock in situ (in place) by weather, plants and animals, with no movement of the material.
The downhill movement of material under gravity, e.g. rockfall, sliding and slumping.
The wearing away of the land by a moving agent such as waves, which carry rock particles.
Erosion by the force of water crashing into cracks, compressing air that then expands and weakens the rock.
Erosion caused by waves hurling rock fragments at a cliff, wearing it away like sandpaper.
Rocks and pebbles carried by the sea collide and wear each other down, becoming smaller and rounder.
The dissolving of soluble rock (e.g. limestone) by sea water or acidic rain.
Mechanical weathering where water freezes in cracks, expands and breaks rock.
Chemical weathering where weak carbonic acid in rainwater dissolves calcium carbonate in limestone and chalk.
The zigzag movement of material along the coast by swash and backwash when waves approach at an angle.
The forward movement of water up a beach after a wave breaks.
The movement of water back down the beach under gravity.
The distance of open water over which the wind blows to create waves.
A low, gentle wave with a strong swash and weak backwash that builds up a beach.
A high, steep wave with a weak swash and strong backwash that erodes a beach.
Transport of large pebbles and boulders by rolling along the sea bed.
Transport of small stones and sand by bouncing along the sea bed.
Transport of fine particles carried within the water.
The dropping of material by the sea when it loses energy.
A stretch of coastline within which movement of sediment is largely self-contained.

worked.ans: Waves approach the coast at an angle because of the prevailing wind (1). The swash carries sand and pebbles up the beach at the same angle as the wave (1). The backwash then carries the material straight back down the beach at right angles to the shore, due to gravity (1). Repeated swash and backwash move the material in a zigzag, so there is a net movement of material along the coast (1). (4 marks)
worked.q: Explain how longshore drift transports material along a coast. (4 marks)
steps: Say how waves approach: at an angle (prevailing wind).
Repeated zigzag leads to net movement.

worked.ans: Constructive waves are low and gentle, whereas destructive waves are high and steep (1). Constructive waves have a strong swash and weak backwash, so they deposit material, but destructive waves have a strong backwash and weak swash, so they remove material (1). Constructive waves therefore build up beaches, while destructive waves erode them (1). Constructive waves are less frequent (about 6 to 8 a minute) than destructive waves (10 to 14 a minute) (1). (4 marks)
worked.q: Compare constructive and destructive waves. (4 marks)
A cliff retreats from 12.0 m to 9.6 m from a fixed marker over 3 years. Calculate the mean annual rate of erosion. (2 marks)
